Issued at 205 PM CDT Sun Sep 27 2026

The morning dense fog event cleared out by late morning across the 
northeastern/east central counties (particularly Hays to Pratt 
corridor), but temperatures have rebounded fairly nicely with 
abundant sunshine outside of some thin high clouds. The 
easter/northeasterly winds, however, will continue into tonight, and 
with lower to mid 60s dewpoints upstream of the surface east-
northeasterly winds, the combined moisture advection and upslope 
component will support another round of fog and low stratus, focused 
especially on the western/northwestern half of the DDC CWA. The 
evening shift will need to monitor observation trends and HRRR 
forecast trends regarding placement and duration of any dense fog 
threat for possible issuance of a Dense Fog Advisory. As of early 
this afternoon, however, there is just enough uncertainty to hoist a 
headline.

After morning fog burns off Monday, surface winds will veer around 
to the southeast, increasing in speed closer to the Colorado line as 
MSLP gradient gradually tightens in advance of the next upper level 
storm system. Monday temperatures should top out in the lower 80s 
most locations (slightly cooler than that north/warmer south). Focus 
Monday night then turns to the incoming polar jet stream trough and 
the remnants of Pacific Hurricane Polo as the two systems phase into 
a larger, eventual extra-tropical cyclone (ETC) somewhere across the 
Southern Rockies and adjacent Southern High Plains. The remnants of 
Polo will draw up plenty of lower-mid tropospheric moisture from the 
Pacific while the increased low level pressure gradient will aid in 
drawing up additional low level gulf moisture from the southeast. 
The merging of these two moisture sources and the phasing of the two 
low pressure systems will work together to result in widespread rain 
and thunderstorms in a significant Warm Conveyor Belt (WCB) air 
stream from northern Mexico straight north across New Mexico into 
southern/southeastern Colorado, the Texas-Oklahoma Panhandles, and 
eventually southwest Kansas.

There is still a rather high degree of confidence in significant 
rainfall across much of southwest and west central Kansas, but there 
is also a fair amount of uncertainty in how these two low pressure 
systems will phase -- when the phasing occurs, how fast the phasing 
occurs, what the resulting combined low pressure system looks like, 
how fast/where the eventual occlusion process occurs -- and related 
to the last point, how fast a dry intrusion air stream (the "dry 
slot") advances north to begin the occlusion and eventual "filling 
of the low" process. Some of the latest deterministic global model 
solutions are now showing a faster occlusion process (i.e. faster 
evolution of dry intrusion working into the low) occurring a little 
farther west, effectively pivoting the low straight north late 
Tuesday Night into Wednesday with a resulting deformation axis 
farther northwest, deeper into Colorado than what models were 
showing yesterday. Regardless, much of southwestern Kansas will see 
heavy rainfall from the main WCB region of the developing ETC when 
low level moisture transport vectors will be the strongest out of 
the south-southeast coincident with PW values well above the 99th 
percentile for this time of year (1.75"+) across much of 
southwestern Kansas. The WCB region alone will likely yield 1.5 to 3 
inches of rain across the southwester/western third to half of the 
DDC CWA given the anomalously high PW values and residence time the 
WCB region will be over any one location across southwest Kansas, 
despite any advancement of the dry slot later on Wednesday.

The latest NWS Weather Prediction Center Excessive Rainfall Outlook 
(ERO) for Day 3 -- Tuesday/Tues. Night will call for SLIGHT Risk 
across all of southwest and west central Kansas with the MODERATE 
Risk clipping the Elkhart to Johnson to Syracuse areas for greater 
risk of torrential rainfall rates leading to a flash flood risk. 
Since there is quite a bit of uncertainty in how the low will 
evolved on Wednesday (even into Thursday), the close proximity of 
the low to southwest Kansas still supports a SLIGHT Risk ERO for Day 
4 -- Wednesday and Day 5 -- Thursday across all of southwest, west 
central, central, and south central Kansas.
